entries.title: South Korea: 16 dead amid record heatwave, President Lee urges action
entries.summary: President Lee Jae Myung called upon officials to take prompt action as extreme weather conditions became "normal". Authorities extended their first-ever heatwave warning ⁠for all of Seoul on Tuesday.
entries.content:
August 4, 2026

President Lee Jae Myung called upon officials to take prompt action as extreme weather conditions became "normal". Authorities extended their first-ever heatwave warning ⁠for all of Seoul on Tuesday.

At least 16 people have died in South Korea, as a record heatwave hits the country. President Lee Jae Myung has called for increased support for those affected amid warnings that extreme weather was becoming more frequent.

Between May 15 and August 2 this year, a total of 2,025 people have suffered heat-related illnesses, the interior ministry said in a statement.

What did President Lee say?

"We need to make efforts for a fundamental overhaul of the national crisis system, ​since this extreme weather is becoming normal," President Lee said at a cabinet meeting, where he urged officials to accelerate measures to protect the daily lives of people. He also called for inspections of ‌power systems as demand for air ‌conditioning rises.

South Korea's southeastern island city of Yangsan recorded a temperature of 42.5 degrees Celsius on ‌Sunday, the highest measured in 122 years of ​observations, the national weather agency said.

After authorities issued their first-ever heatwave warning ⁠for parts of Seoul and Gyeonggi on Monday, the Korea Meteorological Administration extended it to the entire capital city on Tuesday. This was the first such advisory since the designation was introduced this year to alert the public about extreme temperatures.

South Korea grapples with historic heatwave

Temperatures in the capital hit 38 degrees Celsius at midday and were expected to fall only to about 29 degrees overnight. Residents were urged to stay indoors and drink plenty of water. The city has also designated about 4,000 public facilities as cooling centers.

While Seoul has a population of 9.6 million people, the wider metropolitan area is home to more than 25 million residents, which is about half of the country's population.

Scientists have warned that extreme weather events like heatwaves are becoming increasingly frequent and more intense as a result of climate change.  

In Japan, cities have experienced "cruelly hot days" this summer, a new meteorological term the country uses to designate days with intense heat above 40 degrees. Tama Zoo in Tokyo announced Tuesday that three lions have died in the past week due to suspected complications from heatstroke as Japan swelters.

Europe has also faced a sweltering summer, with Germany's heat-related death toll for 2026 already surpassing every full-year total since 2016 — and expected to climb as another spell of extreme temperatures takes hold.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

entries.title: Three lions die of heatstroke at Tokyo zoo
entries.summary: The zoo said that 10 of its 16 lions have been ill. Japan has been experiencing an extreme heatwave since late July.
entries.content:
August 4, 2026

The zoo said that 10 of its 16 lions have been ill. Japan has been experiencing an extreme heatwave since late July.

Tama Zoo in Tokyo announced on Tuesday that three lions have died in the past week due to suspected complications from heatstroke as Japan swelters.

On its website, the zoo said that it was suspending the entire lion exhibit "due to the emergence of several lions requiring treatment for poor health, primarily characterized by loss of appetite, fatigue, and decreased activity... Some lions became severely ill, exhibiting symptoms such as inability to stand and loss of consciousness," before passing away.

Ten of the organization's 16 lions are currently unwell, they said, adding that although lions have evolved to deal with dry African heat, Japanese humidity presents additional challenges.

'Cruelly hot' days

Japan has seen temperatures of 40 degrees Celsius (104 Fahrenheit) in recent weeks, leading to the government to adopt the term "cruelly hot day" for policy-making purposes.

Nearly 18,600 people were treated for heatstroke in Japanese hospitals in late July, national health officials have confirmed, saying that 45 of the victims had already died before they could be treated.

This summer has seen a series of extreme weather events across the globe, which are becoming more frequent as climate change worsens.

Nearby South Korea has also seen a substantial heatwave in recent days, with President Lee Jae

Myung urging authorities to step up support for the population after some 16 people died from heat-related causes.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

entries.title: Germany news: Hedgehog triggers police alert
entries.summary: Police called out after a supermarket burglar alarm went off found an unlikely culprit. Germany's flag carrier, Lufthansa, has turned in poor quarterly results. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Hedgehog triggers police alert

Published August 4, 2026last updated August 4, 2026

Police called out after a supermarket burglar alarm went off found an unlikely culprit. Germany's flag carrier, Lufthansa, has turned in poor quarterly results. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Police attending to a burglary alert at a supermarket say the cause was four-legged and lacking 'criminal energy'
  • Lufthansa profits have plunged in the second quarter

Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Tuesday, August 4, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google

Skip next section German breweries continue to disappear

German breweries continue to disappear

The number of beer breweries in Germany is continuing to sink, a trend possibly reinforced by the falling numbers of people who consume the beverage, new statistics have shown.

In figures released on Tuesday following Friday's International Day of Beer, the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) said there were still 1,415 existing breweries in 2025.

That is 53 fewer than in 2024 and a whole 137 fewer than in 2019, the year in which the most breweries in three decades were registered.

Destatis said declining beer sales were a factor in this development.

They said beer sales had gone down by 15.7% in comparison with 2019.

In 2025, some 7.8 billion liters (2.06 billion US gallons) were sold, down from 8.3 billion liters in 2024 and 9.6 billion liters in 2016.

Of the German states, Bavaria had the most breweries (588), followed by Baden-Württemberg (190) and North Rhine-Westphalia (131).

However, with the exception of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and Saxony-Anhalt, all states have seen the number of breweries decline.

Skip next section Lufthansa profits fall amid soaring fuel prices, industrial action

Lufthansa profits fall amid soaring fuel prices, industrial action

Germany's flag carrier, Lufthansa, says its profits have fallen sharply in the second quarter, citing higher fuel costs, geopolitical instability and employee strikes as reasons for the plunge.

Core profit fell almost 56% to €383 million ($440 million) in comparison with the same period last year, Lufthansa said.

The fall came despite sales rising 10% to €11.1 billion in the three months to the end of June.

Lufthansa said higher fuel prices had increased costs by about €750 million.

"The second quarter was characterized by exceptionally high fuel costs and heightened geopolitical uncertainty," Lufthansa chief financial officer Till Streichert said.

The airline group said it now expects its adjusted earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) to come in at €1.7 billion and €2.2 billion this year.

It had previously predicted that adjusted EBIT would surpass last year's €1.96 billion in spite of the rising cost of fuel amid the Iran war.

Skip next section Police get surprise in supermarket callout

Police get surprise in supermarket callout

Officers who deployed to a supermarket in the town of Mühlheim am Main in the central state of Hesse after a burglar alarm went off in the early hours of the morning did not have to deal with a dangerous criminal but a rather confused animal, police said on Tuesday.

"In the entrance area of the supermarket, the police discovered who had set off the alarm: four-legged, small, round and obviously lacking any criminal energy," they wrote in a statement.

"The suspected 'burglar,' caught in the act, turned out to be a hedgehog that had probably already snuck into the supermarket the day before," they said.

They said the animal was shut into the store by accident at closing time and had ended up "triggering the alarm while off exploring the place."

The hedgehog was briefly examined and found to be unharmed before being set free to continue its nocturnal wanderings, they said.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

A schönen guten Tag from the DW newsroom in Bonn!

We are deep into what in Germany is known as the Sommerloch (summer hole), or "silly season," but we will still be doing our best to bring you some interesting and entertaining reading.

At a time when wars and wildfires are dominating the headlines, news of a hedgehog-triggered police deployment in central Germany could, for example, provide some welcome relief.

But is relief in sight for Germany's best-known airline? The latest news on its finances shows that it is facing some major challenges.

Read on for more.

entries.title: India: Dhaka presses Delhi on stance ahead of Hasina speech
entries.summary: Bangladesh has warned India that hosting the fugitive former leader's political activity could hurt the improving ties between the nations. Meanwhile, Assam continues to battle devastation from floods. DW has more.
entries.content:
India

India: Dhaka presses Delhi on stance ahead of Hasina speech

Published August 4, 2026last updated August 4, 2026

Bangladesh has warned India that hosting the fugitive former leader's political activity could hurt the improving ties between the nations. Meanwhile, Assam continues to battle devastation from floods. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Former Bangladesh leader and fugitive Sheikh Hasina is set to make a speech in Delhi on August 5
  • Dhaka has asked New Delhi to clarify its stance on Hasina's speech
  • Death toll from floods in Assam rise, relief work ongoing

Here's a roundup of the biggest headlines from India on Tuesday, August 4:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section BJP accuses opposition of disrupting Indian parliament

BJP accuses opposition of disrupting Indian parliament

The ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Tuesday accused India's leading opposition party, the Indian National Congress (INC), and its allied parties of disrupting parliamentary sessions and wasting taxpayer money.

"Due to the Congress party's continuous uproar and disruption of the house proceedings, two important bills related to public welfare had to be passed without discussion," BJP national spokesperson Sambit Patra said in a press conference from the party's headquarters.

He was talking about the Registration of Births & Deaths (Amendment) Bill and the Bankers' Books Evidence Bill.

"Both these bills are directly linked to the interests of the public," he said adding that detailed discussions did not take places for either due to the disruption. The bills, however, were passed in the lower house of the parliament.

"Hardly any bill is being discussed. The reason behind this is the conduct of the Congress party and some of its INDIA alliance partners. I am genuinely surprised by their double standards," he told reporters, referring to a broad multiparty alliance led by the iNC, the National Developmental Inclusive Alliance (INDIA).

The BJP's press conference comes amid growing attacks from the opposition regarding the government's response to student protests in July and an alleged theft of donation money from a grand temple in Ayodhya in northern Uttar Pradesh. 

Over the last two weeks, parliamentary sessions have regularly been adjourned due to protests from the opposition bloc or sloganeering in house.

The BJP spokesperson called for INC President Mallikarjun Kharge said India's Home Minister Amit Shah to come to parliament on Monday to explain the reported police brutality on students in last month's protests.

He also called on Prime Minister Narendra Modi to answer how donation money from the temple was stolen when the temple's trust was "under the PM's oversight."

Skip next section Assam death toll from floods rises to 87

Assam death toll from floods rises to 87

Officials in the northeastern state of Assam reported two more deaths on Tuesday, taking the total death toll from the recent flooding to 87.

"Relief efforts continue while rehabilitation gathers pace across the affected districts. We are fully committed to helping every family recover," Assam's Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma said in a post on X.

As per official figures, some 2,281 villages have been affected by the floods and over 73,000 people are currently sheltered in relief camps. Over 16,700 houses have been partially or fully damaged.

Nearly 130,000 people remain affected, even as flood waters are receding from most of the areas, local media reported.

Meanwhile, India's national weather agency has predicted thunderstorms and heavy rainfall in Assam's neighboring states of Arunachal Pradesh and Meghalya over the next few days, warning that it could impact some districts in Assam as well.

Skip next section Dhaka seeks New Delhi's stance ahead of Sheikh Hasina's 'homecoming' speech

Dhaka seeks New Delhi's stance ahead of Sheikh Hasina's 'homecoming' speech

India needs to be clear about its stance on an upcoming speech by ousted Bangladeshi leader Sheikh Hasina, Bangladesh's State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam said, adding that Dhaka did not want the event to adversely impact the improving ties between the neighboring nations.

"We do not want India-Bangladesh relations to be ⁠harmed ​by statements from fugitive accused individuals," she said, adding that India had ​previously indicated it did not expect fugitives to engage in political activities from its territory.

Hasina is set to make a live but virtual speech on August 5, at an event hosted by the Foreign Correspondents' Club of South Asia, titled "Sheikh Hasina's Homecoming."

A flyer for the event, posted on X, said that Hasina would thank journalists at the club in Delhi, ahead of her "homecoming." It will mark the second anniversary of the student-led uprising which toppled her government.

The event is not organised by the Indian government. It is also not Hasina's first public address from India, where she has been living in exile since being ousted from power in Bangladesh in 2024.

Ties between India and Bangladesh grew strained since Hasina fled to the neighboring nation, where she has lived since. While both countries have made attempts at improving ties, Dhaka continues to formally seek Hasina's extradition, which India says is under consideration. 

Meanwhile, Hasina recently told several global news organisations that she planned to return to Bangladesh by December 2026, despite several legal cases and a death sentence.

India's foreign ministry has not publicly responded to Islam's comments yet.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello! and welcome to DW's India blog.

This is Mahima Kapoor reported from New Delhi, and I will be your guide through the noise of fast news coming out of the world's most populous nation.

The weather may be calm in Delhi but not much else is.

Still reeling from the impact of the recent Cockroach movement, the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party is now fielding calls from the opposition, demanding Home Minister Amit Shah explain the reported use of pellet guns on students.

The BJP has, in turn, accused the opposition of disrupting parliamentary proceedings and wasting millions in taxpayer money.

Ties between India and Bangladesh may be under threat again ahead of a planned speech by ousted Bangladeshi leader Sheikh Hasina. While this won't be Hasina's first public address since moving to India in exile, Dhaka has repeatedly objected to her doing so from Indian soil.

In other news, the death toll from the recent flooding int he eastern state of Assam has risen once again, even as flood waters are receding. Meanwhile, the southern state of Kerala has also reported several deaths due to heavy rainfall.

Stay tuned for all of this and more!

entries.title: Venezuela earthquake death toll crosses 6,000
entries.summary: The updated death toll comes weeks after the 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude quakes hit on June 24, causing massive damage to people and property.
entries.content:
August 4, 2026

The updated death toll comes weeks after the 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude quakes hit on June 24, causing massive damage to people and property.

The twin earthquakes that struck Venezuela in late June killed 6,125 people, the latest figures revealed by top lawmaker Jorge Rodriguez on Monday showed.

The updated numbers come weeks after the 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude quakes hit on June 24, unleashing massive damage on people and property, and triggering national emergencies. Unofficial estimates say between 17,000 and 29,500 people are still unaccounted for.

The previous death toll was 5,546.

What was the scale of the damage?

The quake led to nearly 200 buildings collapsing, mostly in the coastal state of La Guaira, which was hit the worst.

Rodríguez said that clean-up operations continued, clearing almost 350,000 tons of debris, which is about 16.5% of the 2.1 million tons of total wreckage estimated by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP).

Authorities classified over 16,200 structures as unsafe, pushing many to leave. Thousands of people are now living in makeshift shelters in La Guaira and Caracas.

On Friday, lawmakers in the country unanimously approved a law that makes it easier to rent properties, a measure aimed at helping displaced victims. It repeals an anti-rental legislation passed by former leftist administrations.

Venezuela's Acting President ​Delcy Rodriguez came to power after US forces kidnapped her predecessor Nicolas Maduro in January and took him to New York, where he is facing trial. She has defended the government amid criticism ​that officials did not do enough to help ⁠quake victims, including people trapped in the rubble.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Cuba: Further blackouts disrupt energy restoration attempts
entries.summary: Authorities say unfavorable weather in the Caribbean has hampered efforts to restore power to Cuba's national grid amid repeated blackouts. Many Cubans now have power only for a few hours a day.
entries.content:
Cuba

Cuba: Further blackouts disrupt energy restoration attempts

August 4, 2026

Authorities say unfavorable weather in the Caribbean has hampered efforts to restore power to Cuba's national grid amid repeated blackouts. Many Cubans now have power only for a few hours a day.

Cuba's efforts to restore electricity after a series of blackouts were hampered again on Monday when a second nationwide power cut in a day, the sixth this year, struck its national grid.

Power began returning to parts of Havana and several provinces in central and western Cuba during Monday and, by midday, authorities said about half of the capital had electricity again.

However, the state electricity provider later warned that unfavorable weather had again interrupted the restoration process.

Cuba blackouts: What have authorities said?

"In the process of reestablishing the [National Electric System], existing weather events caused disruptions to the grid, directly affecting the generator units that were online," the provider said in a statement posted to social media on Monday afternoon, without specifying the extent of damage or how many areas were affected.

"We continue to work intensively to revert the situation and achieve the system reset as soon as possible."

By early evening, authorities were reporting some progress, saying four generating units at Energas Jaruco were operating and several transmission substations around Havana had ​been re-energized.

Cuba: Life amid blackouts

Repeated blackouts ⁠since the start of the year have ​disrupted businesses, public services and life in general across Cuba, a Caribbean ​island of roughly 10 million people.

Most Cubans now have power only for a few hours a day at best, making normal life nearly impossible.

The government, which is already battling shortages of food, fuel ​and medicine and a long economic downturn, blames decades of United States sanctions and embargoes which limit access ​to fuel, financing and ⁠spare parts needed to maintain its power system.

The Trump administration has this year tightened sanctions and enacted an oil embargo, further choking the Caribbean country.

Washington claims the outages reflect failures of ⁠the country's state-run economic model.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: US: 25 states sue over Trump's new tariffs
entries.summary: The coalition of largely Democratic-led states is challenging the Trump administration's argument that tariffs will address imports produced by alleged "forced labor" abroad. The White House insists the move is legal.
entries.content:
United States of America

US: 25 states sue over Trump's new tariffs

August 4, 2026

The coalition of largely Democratic-led states is challenging the Trump administration's argument that tariffs will address imports produced by alleged "forced labor" abroad. The White House insists the move is legal.

Twenty-five US states sued President Donald Trump's administration Monday over its latest tariffs, saying they were a pretext for replacing import taxes struck down by the Supreme Court in February.

The United States imposed double-digit tariffs on 59 countries plus the European Union last month, accusing them of not doing enough to crack down on imports produced by forced labor.

The new tariffs took effect just as the clock ran out on temporary tariffs President Trump had turned to after the Supreme Court defeat.

What did the 25 states say in their lawsuit against Trump tariffs?

"After losing at the Supreme Court, the administration is once again trying to illegally raise taxes on families and businesses with a new round of tariffs," said New York Attorney General Letitia James, launching the lawsuit.

"Despite losing every step of the way, Trump is trying yet again to inflict more on working families and homegrown businesses," added Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield.

Joining New York and Oregon in the legal action were the Democratic-led states of Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Kentucky, Massachusetts, Maryland, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Virginia, Washington and Wisconsin – plus Republican-led Nevada and Vermont.

"There is no rational fit between the purported problem of forced labor in international supply chains and the blanket global tariffs," the coalition of states argued in their court filing.

White House insists Trump tariffs are legal

Since taking office for his second term, Trump has argued that US trading partners have been taking advantage of the world's largest economy, and has sought to use tariffs as leverage to strike new trade deals.

His administration has upended global trade by imposing wide-ranging tariffs – often at eye-watering levels – against Washington's friends and foes alike.

The latest tariffs, invoked under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, range from 10% to 12.5% and hit countries that account for 99% of American imports.

"The Tariff Action is arbitrary, capricious and contrary to law," the lawsuit said, but the White House hit back, insisting that the government move was legal.

"The United States is using its lawful authority to obtain the elimination of unreasonable acts, policies, and practices that burden US commerce," said White House spokesman Kush Desai.

"A foreign country's failure to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor is unreasonable and burdens US commerce, including American workers, and must be addressed."

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Study shows why younger generations may be more cancer-prone
entries.summary: Researchers are observing certain age-related types of cancer more frequently in younger people. A new study suggests this could be because younger generations are aging faster than their parents or grandparents.
entries.content:
August 3, 2026

Researchers are observing certain age-related types of cancer more frequently in younger people. A new study suggests this could be because younger generations are aging faster than their parents or grandparents.

Susanna was just 28 years old when she was diagnosed with bowel cancer. Andre developed lung cancer when he was only 34. Both of them have turned to social media to talk about their fight against the disease. Neither of them are medical outliers — not anymore.

The German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ) has reported a sharp increase in gastrointestinal cancer cases for patients between the ages of 20 and 39. In the US, researchers have observed a similar development, with an even higher disease ratio than in Germany. Younger people are also increasingly being diagnosed with other types of cancers, including those that affect patients' bone marrow or uterus. 

Cancer is usually regarded as an age-related disease. According to the German Cancer Aid non-profit, the average age for men and women with cancer is around 69. Cancer cells form when certain sections of the genetic sequence mutate and can no longer be repaired. The older we get, the less reliable our repair system becomes.

Gap between chronologal and biological gap increasing

A study by researchers at Washington University School of Medicine, US, has now found a link that could help explain why an increasing number of people under 50 are developing early-onset cancer. The reason, they suggest, is that younger generations are displaying a wider gap between their biological and their chronological ages. In short, they are aging faster.

While the chronological age counts how many years have passed since a person's birth, their biological age describes how much their body has aged, based on the cellular damage accumulated. Individual organs and tissues can age at varying speeds.

In other words, the same person's liver, heart and brain could each have different biological ages, all of which could differ still from the person's actual age.

The recent study has now for the first time established a link between the increasing gap between biological and chronological ages in younger generations on the one hand, and the risk of early-onset cancer on the other, Ron Jachimowicz explains. He's an attending physician and hematologist at the University Hospital Cologne, as well as head of the Max Planck Research Group for Biology of Aging.

"Don't forget, this is a correlative study," Jachomowicz cautions.

Correlation refers to two things appearing in concert, so it looks like they are related. It does not prove causation, which we speak of when one factor causes another.

While results can provide certain indications that seem quite plausible, researchers were already well aware of the fact "that there is an association between biological age and the risk of developing cancer," Jachomowicz says.

DNA, bloodmarkers and telomeres: How to determine one's biological age

It's not easy to determine a person's biological age. Calculating it requires a number of parameters — there is no single, precise test. Instead, epigenetic tests are used to determine chemical alterations of DNA sequences, evaluating certain blood values and measuring the length of so-called telomeres — that is, the repetitive DNA sequence located at the end of chromosomes that function as protective caps.

There are also physiological tests, to monitor various body and organ functions, as well as cognitive evaluations.

Researchers in the study at hand applied a combination of these various measurement techniques to analyze the data of more than 150,000 individuals drawn from the UK Biobank, a British biometric dataset.

They found that people born between 1965 and 1974 had a significantly higher gap between their chronological and biological ages than people born between 1950 and 1954. The younger the cohort examined, the wider that gap appeared to grow.

An investigation involving more than 10,000 US individuals revealed an even higher deviation for participants born between 1990 and 1999, compared to a cohort born between 1965 and 1969.

"In Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom (UK) and the US, people born in the 1990s face at least fourfold higher risk of early-onset colorectal cancer compared with those in the 1960s," the authors write in the study.

Can I improve my biological age?

We used to assume that a healthy lifestyle could make up 75% to 90% of one's biological age. Now we know that's not true, Jachimowicz explains.

"We can influence about 50% of it," he says, "while the other 50% are genetically predetermined."

To help slow the aging process, he recommends "typical lifestyle interventions," such as working out regularly, eating a balanced diet, getting enough sleep, and avoiding drugs and alcohol. 

And the value of social contacts should not be underestimated, he adds.

It's not easy to say why, on a biological level, younger generations are aging faster than their parents and grandparents. But there are a few hypotheses.

"Younger people are being exposed to earlier and longer obesity," says Tanwei Yuan, an epidemiologist in the Department of Clinical Epidemiology and Aging Research of the DKFZ in Heidelberg.

Other contributing factors are a sedentary lifestyle, and poor sleep quality due to extended periods of time in front of a screen, Yuan adds. She says the current study delivers valuable insights that confirm hypotheses long held by cancer researchers.

She also stresses the value of a healthy lifestyle to help reduce the risk of early-onset cancer.

"If you feel unwell, go to a doctor and ask for the screening," Yuan recommends.

Yuan knows what she's talking about. The 32-year-old researcher says she had felt unwell for quite some time before being diagnosed with intestinal polyps last year. While these can start out benign, if left untreated, polyps can become cancerous. That's why it's important to listen closely to your body and take measures early, she says.

Can my doctor determine my biological age?

In a word: no, says Jachimowicz.

Determining an individual's biological age is the "subject of current scientific research, but in no way a practical routine or part of everyday clinical work."

However, he believes it should be, especially when it comes to initiating early cancer interventions. He believes this current study is particularly valuable because it highlights this path forward for future studies.

"It's still far off in the future," he says, "but it's very exciting."

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: Dry Danube River threatens nuclear power in Romania, Hungary
entries.summary: Hungary's Paks nuclear power plant was operating at about 10% of capacity because of a lack of cooling riverwater. In Romania, the military blew up a rock outcrop in a bid to improve water flow to the Cernavoda plant.
entries.content:
August 3, 2026

Hungary's Paks nuclear power plant was operating at about 10% of capacity because of a lack of cooling river water. In Romania, the military blew up a rock outcrop in a bid to improve water flow to the Cernavoda plant.

Several central and eastern European countries are facing power shortages and impacts on industry amid prolonged hot and dry weather and record low levels on the Danube River and other waterways. 

Hungary narrowly averted switching off its lone nuclear plant, but had still powered it down to a fraction of capacity. In Romania, the navy demolished a rocky outcrop exposed in the Danube's riverbed, trying to improve the water flow. 

And in Serbia, hydroelectric power output was severely impacted by the dry conditions. 

Continued hot and dry weather is forecast during the week, providing little sign of relief.

How did Romania try to feed the Cernavoda power plant?

Romania's military detonated a rocky outcrop exposed by the low water levels on a branch of the Danube, seeking to improve the flow of cooling water to the Cernavoda nuclear plant, which typically supplies about one-fifth of the country's power.

The plant draws all of its cooling water from the Danube.

Soldiers detonated a rock some 50 kilometers (roughly 30 miles) upstream. The debris would be taken to a strategic spot and sunk to help raise the water level.

Defense Minister Radu Miruta said the operation was a success and the military had been waiting for a chance to access and demolish the rocks for decades.

If the partial diversion of the water fails, Miruta said, the plant would likely have to shut down entirely by Thursday.

Caretaker Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan said that carmakers Dacia and Ford had agreed to suspend production in Romania until August 19, following a crisis meeting with representatives of the energy-intensive industry. He said that other companies would be taking similar steps.

What was the situation at Hungary's Paks power plant?

Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar said it was possible to avoid the unprecedented total shutdown of the Paks nuclear power plant on Monday that was originally announced last week. 

But the four-reactor station that typically generates almost half of Hungary's electricity production and around a third of its consumption was running at little more than 10% capacity on Monday.

Hungary had asked industrial users to curb consumption and households to make voluntary savings. Electric-powered freight trains were also stopped on Monday to reduce the load on the grid.

Magyar thanked people for their restraint on Monday evening.

"We have entered the critical period. The network is stable, consumption is currently well below planned levels, thanks to self-restraint. The last Paks turbine is operational. I will report back shortly from the (grid operator) MAVIR control room," he said.

Magyar also said slightly earlier on Monday that "water management forecasts for the coming days have become slightly more optimistic."

How was Serbia affected?

In Serbia, the vast Iron Gate hydroelectric plant on the Danube was operating at only around one-fifth capacity on Monday.

Prime Minister Djuro Macut convened an emergency meeting on Monday to discuss the energy problems.

He appealed to residents to "minimize the use of big consumers of electricity in their homes, such as air conditioners," having described the situation as "serious and demanding" late on Sunday.

Far upstream in Bavaria, the Danube's levels were also affecting freight transport. 

New German Transport Minister Steffen Bilger said the historic low levels on the Danube, and particularly the Rhine to the west — Europe's busiest inland freight waterway — were providing a first challenge for his tenure. 

"It is indeed a very tense situation with the low waters," Bilger told Reuters TV on Monday, saying he would chair a crisis meeting on Thursday. "We are used to repeated low water situations, but this is really a very early point in the calendar year for problems of the kind we're currently experiencing."

Typically European rivers reach their lowest levels slightly later in the summer — it's entirely possible that several more weeks of predominantly hot and dry weather are yet to come.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: Iran war: Trump tells Iranian leaders to make deal or surrender
entries.summary: President Donald Trump declared that the US military blockade would continue until Iran either made a deal or went for "total surrender."

Iran war: Trump tells Iranians to make deal or surrender

Published August 3, 2026last updated August 4, 2026

President Donald Trump declared that the US military blockade would continue until Iran either made a deal or went for "total surrender."

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

This blog, covering the latest developments in the US-Israel war with Iran and the wider fallout across the Middle East, has now closed. Read below for an overview of the top headlines on Monday, August 3:

  • Trump calls Iran's leaders 'duplicitous,' tells them to make deal or surrender

  • Iran and Oman plan new route for Strait of Hormuz vessels, Tehran says

  • Cargo vessel 'hit by unknown projectile' off Oman's coast, UKMTO says

  • Trump says new round of Iran talks set for Monday

  • Iran says there are no talks underway with Washington

  • Two tankers with Saudi oil exit Red Sea

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Cargo vessel 'hit by unknown projectile' off Oman's coast, UKMTO says

Cargo vessel 'hit by unknown projectile' off Oman's coast, UKMTO says

The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said it had received a report of an incident off the coast of Oman.

The report, dated Monday but released on Tuesday, said the incident occurred 20 nautical miles northeast of Oman's Al Khasab.

"A cargo vessel has broadcasted on VHF 16 that they have been hit by an unknown projectile," UKMTO said on X, adding that authorities were looking into the incident.

Skip next section Trump threatens Iran with 'decapitation' if no deal is reached

Trump threatens Iran with 'decapitation' if no deal is reached

US President Donald Trump insisted that negotiations with Iran were ongoing, adding that the Islamic Republic was facing a "last chance before decapitation."

Trump told reporters at the White House that he agreed to continue to pursue talks with Iran at the request of Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and other countries.

But Iran's foreign ministry has so far denied that negotiations with Washington were taking place.

"We are talking right now," Trump said.

"This is a last chance for them to sign a good document," the US president added. "I want to give them every last chance before decapitation."

The remarks were similar to last week's threat by Trump that Iran would be hit "very hard," facing potentially with renewed attacks against energy infrastructure. But the US president backed down later, saying the "perimeters" of a deal were there.

Skip next section Board of Peace: Gaza deal possible only with 'complete' Hamas disarmament

Board of Peace: Gaza deal possible only with 'complete' Hamas disarmament

US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace said that an Israeli withdrawal in Gaza requires the militant group Hamas's "complete" disarmament.

The board made the statement on the social media platform X, following a meeting with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

"We note that the full withdrawal of the IDF beyond the Yellow Line will take place only once decommissioning (of weapons) is complete, as Hamas committed to the mediators," the board wrote, making reference to a line between the area under Hamas control and that held by the Israeli army.

"Israel and the Board of Peace share a common understanding of the ultimate objectives," the statement added.

Meanwhile, Netanyahu's office said Israel demanded concrete disarmament by Hamas.

"Israel has conveyed its comments and concerns on the proposed framework to our American counterparts. The version that has been made public does not reflect Israel's positions," Doron Spielman, spokesman for the prime minister's office, told the AFP news agency.

Skip next section Trump calls Iran's leaders 'duplicitous,' tells them to make deal or surrender

Trump calls Iran's leaders 'duplicitous,' tells them to make deal or surrender

US President Donald Trump lashed out at Iran, criticizing it for seeking to work directly with Oman on a solution to the backlog in the Strait of Hormuz.

"Iranian Leadership is unbelievably duplicitous! They ask for a meeting, some would say 'beg,' talks begin, with more scheduled in the immediate future, and they say, openly and proudly, that they’re not having any discussions, that nothing is being talked about, and they’re only dealing with 'Oman,'" Trump wrote on his social media platform Truth Social.

The remarks come after Iran announced it was negotiating a joint temporary shipping corridor with Oman.

Trump asserted, however, that the Strait of Hormuz is "already completely controlled by the United States Navy" and the blockade it has imposed on it.

"Nothing gets through to Iran, unless we want it to, and nothing will get through, unless a Deal, or Total Surrender, is accomplished," Trump wrote.

The US president also again vowed that Iran would not obtain a nuclear weapon.

Skip next section Tehran: Iran and Oman plan new route for Strait of Hormuz vessels

Tehran: Iran and Oman plan new route for Strait of Hormuz vessels

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said the country is negotiating a joint temporary shipping corridor in the strategically important Strait of Hormuz with Oman.

According to the state news agency IRNA the idea would involve a circular route rather than several separate lanes until a final arrangement was reached.

The announcement comes after US President Donald Trump announced a new round of talks with Iranian representative.

Under the plan, tankers or cargo ships would enter the Strait of Hormuz on a northern route through Iranian territorial waters.

After calling at ports in Iran or in Arab Gulf states, the ships would use a southern route through Omani territorial waters for the return journey.

Skip next section Iran hangs two convicted of espionage

Iran hangs two convicted of espionage

Iran says it executed two men on Monday after they were convicted of spying for Israel.

It is the latest in a series of hangings on espionage allegations carried out by Tehran since the start of the war with Israel and the US in late February.

"Omid Behzad and Pouria Safvat were hanged this morning for transmitting the coordinates of sensitive military and security sites to Mossad agents," said Mizan, the media outlet for Iran's judiciary.

Mossad is Israel's foreign intelligence service.

"They helped the intelligence services achieve their objectives by providing them with information on military and security centres during the war," Mizan added.

Executions in Iran as a whole have risen since the war broke out.

According to Amnesty International and several other rights groups, the country carries out the second-highest number of executions in the world, after China.

At least 1,639 people were executed in Iran last year, a record high since 1989, according to the Norway-based NGO Iran Human Rights and Together Against the Death Penalty (ECPM), which has its headquarters in Paris.

Skip next section Oil slumps on hopes of Iran deal

Oil slumps on hopes of Iran deal

Oil prices fell sharply in early Asian trading after US President Donald Trump announced new talks with Iran aimed at ending the Middle East conflict and reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

Brent crude for September delivery dropped more than 6% to $82.41 a barrel in early trade.

The conflict has disrupted energy markets and effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global oil and gas shipment

Skip next section No current talks with US — Iranian Foreign Ministry

No current talks with US — Iranian Foreign Ministry

Iran is not currently conducting talks with the ‌US, the Iranian Foreign Ministry said on Monday, adding that it is, however, in discussions with Oman about a temporary safe route through the Strait of Hormuz.

The remarks by ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei came after US President Donald Trump said new talks with Iran on a peace deal were set to begin on Monday.

"We are not currently negotiating with the United States. Our negotiations are with Oman to secure passage through the Strait of Hormuz," Baghaei said during a weekly press briefing.

He added that a deal with Oman would not be enough to reopen the strait for commercial shipping, as the situation would stay unchanged if the US continued with its "aggression."

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

We are continuing our coverage on the US war with Iran and broader developments in the Middle East after US President Donald Trump said he had called off strikes on the West Asian country.

He later told reporters that Washington and Tehran were to carry out new talks on Monday. There was no immediate response from Iran.

Meanwhile, some Saudi oil ships passed through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait despite a stated embargo by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militia.

Stay with us for all this and more.

Skip next section Some Saudi oil shipments get through Bab el-Mandeb

Some Saudi oil shipments get through Bab el-Mandeb

Two tankers carrying Saudi crude successfully crossed the Bab el-Mandeb Strait over the weekend, despite security concerns and a Houthi-declared maritime embargo against Saudi Arabia.

Shipping data showed traffic through the waterway fell sharply amid the heightened security risks, with just 18 commodity vessels passing on Sunday, down from 28 on Friday.

The tankers, Lesvos and Desh Vaibhav, transited with their Automatic Identification System (AIS) tracking systems switched off, the Kpler data showed. Together, they were carrying about three million barrels of Saudi oil.

Desh Vaibhav is heading to India's Sikka port, while Lesvos' destination remains unclear.

Meanwhile, vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz also slowed, with commodity crossings dropping after reports of multiple tanker attacks.

The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency says three more attacks have been reported since Saturday, raising fresh concerns over the security of key global energy shipping routes.

What is the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis?

The Houthis are an Iran-backed militant group that has controlled most of Yemen's more populous areas — including the capital, Sanaa — for a little over a decade.

A coalition led by Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen in 2015 in support of the country's internationally recognized government, which is de facto based in the southern city of Aden.

While the Saudi-backed government agreed to a truce with the Houthis in 2022, this year tensions have risen again amid the US war with Iran.

Skip next section Trump says Iran talks to resume amid push to reopen Strait of Hormuz

Trump says Iran talks to resume amid push to reopen Strait of Hormuz

US President Donald Trump said new talks with Iran are set to begin on Monday after he decided to hold off on striking the Islamic republic to pursue a deal to end the war.

"They said we would much prefer a deal as opposed to an attack, because you don't know where these attacks lead," Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One late on Sunday.

He was looking for a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and address concerns over Tehran's nuclear program.

He gave no details on the venue, participants, or any deadline for an agreement.

The comments followed a social media post in which Trump said Iran and other Middle Eastern countries had requested more time to complete a deal.

Iranian media denied that Tehran had asked Trump not to strike.

Iran and the United States agreed in mid-June on a framework deal to end the war, with details to be finalized during a 60-day transition period, but both sides have since carried out major attacks.
